description: This module explores the Limitation Act, 1963, which sets strict time limits for initiating legal actions. It covers the foundational maxims of limitation, the critical distinction between barring a remedy versus extinguishing a right, and the rules regarding the condonation of delay.

key_points: Objective: The law of limitation rests on two public policy maxims: (1) 'Interest reipublicae ut sit finis litium' (It is in the interest of the State that there should be an end to litigation) and (2) 'Vigilantibus non dormientibus jura subveniunt' (The law assists those who are vigilant with their rights, and not those that sleep thereupon).

Bar of Limitation (Section 3): The Act mandates that every suit, appeal, and application filed after the prescribed period of limitation shall be dismissed by the court, even if the defendant has not raised limitation as a defense.

remedy_vs_right.concept: Bars the Remedy, Not the Right
key_points: General Rule: The expiry of the limitation period typically bars the judicial 'remedy' (the ability to file a lawsuit), but it does not extinguish the underlying legal 'right'. For example, a time-barred debt cannot be recovered in court, but the debt itself still legally exists and can be adjusted against other dues.

Exception - Adverse Possession (Section 27): An exception to the general rule is property rights. Under Section 27, if a person fails to file a suit for possession of any property within the limitation period (usually 12 years), their actual ownership 'right' to that property is completely extinguished, and the possessor gains title by 'prescription'.

Sufficient Cause: Under Section 5, a court has the discretionary power to admit an appeal or an application after the expiry of the limitation period if the applicant can prove they had a 'sufficient cause' for not filing it on time.

Exclusion of Suits: Crucially, Section 5 (Condonation of Delay) applies only to appeals and applications. It does NOT apply to original 'suits'. A time-barred civil suit cannot be admitted under any circumstances, regardless of the cause for delay.

questions.question: A creditor fails to file a lawsuit to recover a loan within the 3-year limitation period. According to the general principles of the Limitation Act, what is the legal status of this debt?

options.A: Both the right to the debt and the legal remedy to recover it in court are destroyed.
options.B: The legal remedy to sue in court is barred, but the underlying right to the debt remains alive.
options.C: The debt becomes a criminal offense.
options.D: The creditor can automatically extend the limitation period by sending a legal notice.

questions.explanation: A fundamental rule of the Limitation Act is that limitation 'bars the remedy, but does not extinguish the right'. The creditor can no longer use the court to force repayment (remedy), but the debt itself still exists legally.

questions.question: An individual meets with a severe accident and remains in a coma for several months, causing them to miss the deadline to file an original civil suit for breach of contract. They apply to the court for a 'condonation of delay' under Section 5 of the Limitation Act, citing medical emergencies as a 'sufficient cause'. Will the court admit the suit?

options.A: Yes, because a coma is universally accepted as a 'sufficient cause' for delay.
options.B: Yes, but they will have to pay a hefty penalty to the court.
options.C: No, because Section 5 of the Limitation Act (Condonation of Delay) does not apply to original suits, regardless of the reason.
options.D: No, because medical emergencies are not covered under the Limitation Act.

questions.explanation: Section 5 of the Limitation Act explicitly allows for the condonation of delay only for appeals and applications. It strictly does not apply to the filing of original 'suits'. Once the limitation period for an original suit expires, it is permanently barred.

questions.question: A trespasser occupies an empty plot of land. The true owner is aware of this but takes no legal action to evict the trespasser for 15 years. Under Section 27 of the Limitation Act (which prescribes a 12-year period for property recovery), what happens to the true owner's legal rights?

options.A: The owner's remedy to sue is barred, but they remain the legal owner of the land forever.
options.B: The owner's right to the property is completely extinguished, and the trespasser acquires ownership by 'prescription'.
options.C: The land automatically becomes government property.
options.D: The owner can evict the trespasser but cannot claim past rent.

questions.explanation: While limitation generally only bars the remedy, Section 27 creates an exception for property. If an owner fails to sue for possession within the limitation period (12 years), not only is their remedy barred, but their fundamental 'right' to the property is completely extinguished. The trespasser acquires legal title through 'adverse possession' or 'prescription'.
